sections.heading: Console guide
sections.text:
A plain-language guide to the Fleetwright operator console: what each screen shows, what the states
mean and what to do when something looks wrong. The console's help assistant answers from this
guide and the other published documentation.

sections.heading: Console guide — What you are looking at
sections.text:
Fleetwright runs a fleet of browser workers that watch a job board, hold exactly one claim per matching job,
and crawl catalogues. The public workspace runs against an **owned freight exchange**: a
load board owned and operated by this project, so nothing commercial is booked and no third-party site is touched.

Anonymous visitors get a **read-only, redacted** view of the public workspace: emails and client addresses
are masked. The public workspace login (shown on the sign-in page) adds the workspace controls. Staff
accounts sign in with a password and a one-time code from an authenticator app.

Roles, from least to most access: **Visitor** (anonymous, read-only), **Viewer** and **Guest**
(signed-in, read-only; Guest can use workspace controls), **Operator** (can change filters and enter
one-time codes), **Owner** (everything, including workflow approvals and access grants). The server
checks the role on every request; hiding a button is never the only protection.

sections.heading: Console guide — Overview
sections.text:
Claims by state over the last hour, worker health and alerts. **Healthy** workers sent a heartbeat
recently; **stale** ones missed several; **dead** ones stopped answering. Alerts appear for stale
workers, sessions that need attention, and claims being reconciled.

sections.heading: Console guide — Workers
sections.text:
Every browser worker slot, its cell, mode (watcher or claimer), account and last heartbeat. Slots
stopped on purpose during a redeploy are not counted as missing. A worker is killed and replaced
safely at any time: it keeps no state of its own.

sections.heading: Console guide — Accounts & sessions
Console guide — Filters
sections.text:
Which loads the fleet tries to claim: origin, destination, minimum rate, equipment and weight.
Filters are data. Every edit is versioned, written to the audit log and reloaded by the dispatchers
immediately, without a restart.

sections.heading: Console guide — Schedules
sections.text: Time-zone-aware windows that switch filters and accounts on and off.

sections.heading: Console guide — Claims
sections.text:
Every detected load and what happened to it, with the full state timeline:

- **QUEUED** — a detection matched a filter; exactly one claim exists for that job.
- **LEASED** — one worker holds the claim with a fencing token until the lease expires.
- **ACTING** — that worker is sending the booking now.
- **CONFIRMED** / **FAILED** — the board gave a definite answer.
- **UNKNOWN** — the booking may have happened but the answer was lost (for example the worker died
  mid-action). Fleetwright never retries an UNKNOWN claim blindly, because a retry could book twice.
- **RECONCILED** — the reconciler asked the board what the account really booked and recorded it.

If you see UNKNOWN claims, that is the system being honest about uncertainty, not a failure. They
normally move to RECONCILED within seconds. One that stays UNKNOWN needs a human to check.

sections.heading: Console guide — Latency
sections.text:
Each stage is measured separately: board publish → detection, detection → queued → leased → action
sent → confirmed. Publish→detect is never averaged into detect→action, so you can see where time goes.
Percentiles (p50/p95/p99) are over the recent window.

sections.heading: Console guide — Crawl jobs
sections.text:
Crawls are defined as data (seeds, scope rules, extractors). Each cycle reports item counts; a sudden
drop or zero results raises an alarm, which catches silent page-layout changes. Exports are private.

sections.heading: Console guide — Browser workflows
sections.text:
Approved, versioned workflows that AI clients can request through the scoped MCP interface. Risky
actions wait for an exact owner approval; access grants are scoped, expire and can be revoked.

sections.heading: Console guide — Audit log
sections.text:
Append-only. Every change and every claim action is recorded with who, what and when. Visitors see
it redacted.

sections.heading: Console guide — Workspace controls
sections.text:
Signed in with the public workspace login, you can start a capped load burst (a few minutes, rate
limited) and inject faults on the owned board: rate limits, server errors, slow responses, forced
session expiry, a layout change and competing bots. Settings reset themselves after a while. Then
watch Claims, Latency and the Overview react.

sections.heading: Console guide — Common questions
sections.text:
**Why did a claim fail?** Usually another bot booked the load first, the board returned an error,
or the lease ran out before acting. The claim's timeline shows the step and the reason.

**Can two workers book the same load?** No. Postgres allows exactly one claim per job, and a fencing
token rejects any worker that lost its lease. See the claim lifecycle and ADR 0001.

**Is the data live?** The header says **Live** with **Live updates** when the event stream is
connected, or "Refreshing every N s" while it reconnects. The static reference build says it shows offline reference data.

**What is measured and what is a target?** Measured results include 50 and 70 browser contexts sustained
for an hour on one PC (fixture pages, not authenticated freight workers) and the recorded test runs. 1M+ console users and 99.9% availability are design
targets with a documented path, not measured results; the public workspace runs on one shared server.

**Who do I contact?** Open an issue on the public GitHub repository. Report security problems as
described in SECURITY.md, not in an issue.

sections.heading: Console guide — The help assistant
sections.text:
The assistant is an AI. It answers from this documentation and from read-only console data your
role can already see; it cannot change anything. It can be wrong, so check important answers against
the linked sources. When the AI is unavailable or the daily AI budget is used up, it shows the most
relevant documentation passages instead. Questions are not stored by Fleetwright; the AI provider
processes them to produce an answer (see the privacy notes).

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations
sections.text:
Fleetwright coordinates authorized browser work through durable ownership, exact-action approval
and destination evidence. It combines a warm browser fleet, scoped MCP supervision, catalogue
crawling and a separate local model-assisted browser application.

**Open Fleetwright** ·
**Documentation** · **Installation** ·
**API and MCP**

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Capabilities
sections.text:
| Capability | Included behavior |
| Coordinated browser fleet | Watcher/actor separation, warm sessions, fenced claims, database-clock account pacing, filters, schedules and execution cells |
| Approved workflows | Freight booking and maintenance requests; owner approval binds tenant, account, inputs and the full versioned contract |
| MCP supervision | Six bounded stdio tools with separate observe/execute grants, expiry and immediate revocation checks |
| Catalogue crawler | Durable frontier, same-origin definitions, pinned HTTP/TLS egress, JSON/CSS extraction, quality alarms, retention and private JSONL export |
| Local browser agent | SQLite and installed Ollama model, three maintained form workflows, exact approvals, receipts, cancellation and isolated optional CDP |
| Console help assistant | AI answers from the published docs and the read-only data the visitor's role can see; disclosed as AI, marked machine-readably, no write tools, per-user limits and a daily budget, documentation-search fallback (console guide) |
| Operations | Authenticated metrics, renewable observe-only collection, independent public probes, verified archives and encrypted off-host recovery |
| Release assurance | Immutable source/artifact inventory, final-image SBOM/scans, offline signatures, rehearsal, compatibility-aware rollback and hash parity |

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Capabilities
sections.text:
The console separates private owner authority from public read-only access and capped shared
workspace controls. Its freight exchange and maintenance portal are owned destinations with
independent receipt records. A new customer destination requires explicit authorization, a reviewed
contract and its own behavioral evidence. The hosted agent page links to an application on your
computer; it does not control your browser remotely.

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Evidence and current boundary
sections.text:
The deployed frontend/backend release is `20261015-publication-rc1`, built from source `cd64e6b`.
Exact rehearsal, native server image checks, independent artifact review, public workflows,
operator UI and HTTP checks passed. All 146 deployed manifest entries and eight application/web
service-role image identities matched the signed release. Verification is maintained in the
release record.

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Evidence and current boundary
sections.text:
Release source `cd64e6b` updates public documentation and the central distinct web-image tag;
business runtime behavior is unchanged from the 14 October browser-supervision correction.
The final complete suite ran after local builds/rehearsal finished, with its generated dashboard
prerequisite frozen alongside runtime/configuration. Driver-loss supervision and readiness prevent

Historical owned-board latency was approximately 365 ms p50 / 540 ms p95 from detection to

testing and capacity evidence.
The deployment has a single-host failure domain. 1M+ simultaneous control-plane users
and 99% / 99.9% availability objectives are future design and validation
targets. Arbitrary-site exactly-once execution and measured monthly availability are not established.

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Install and run
sections.text:
Use Python 3.12, uv, Docker Compose and Node.js 24 for the full workspace:

Continue with local development to start the owned destination,
seed accounts, then start the API, gateway, control loop and workers. Run the dashboard from
`apps/dashboard`. Use separate local
credentials and preserve existing data volumes.

For the standalone agent, follow the local-agent guide.
It needs SQLite, Playwright Chromium and an installed local Ollama model; PostgreSQL, Redis,
Docker and paid model APIs are not runtime requirements.

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Integration and operating contract
sections.text:
Environment-specific settings have one typed boundary:
`fw_core.settings`, documented in
configuration and `.env.example`.
Maintained destination contracts, prompts and product data live in `config/`; secrets stay private.

MCP clients submit proposals and inspect evidence. They cannot grant themselves authority or approve
their own work. Owners review exact proposals in the console. A changed, expired, revoked or consumed
approval cannot authorize an action. Interrupted actions remain `UNKNOWN` until matching receipts
resolve them; redeployment, cancellation and a missing response do not undo a destination action.

Before onboarding, review product scope, acceptable use,
privacy, security controls and the license.
Operational support, commercial terms and service-level commitments require a separate agreement.

sections.heading: Fleetwright — Reliable Browser Operations — Product delivery and operating ownership
sections.text:
Public documentation is maintained across the complete workspace. Start with the
documentation index, then use service ownership
to map each process to its startup, authority, health and recovery responsibilities.
Data lifecycle covers records, evidence, exports and archives;
commercial readiness defines destination permission,
licensing, privacy, support and release acceptance before customer onboarding.

The future design targets **1M+ simultaneous authorized console users**, with a **99% initial
operating objective** and **99.9% multi-zone objective**. The
validation plan specifies tiered workload, resource, failure,
recovery and error-budget gates. Execution cells retain separate destination/account budgets.
Current measurements stay in dated release records. Source, signed artifacts, runtime behavior,
operational recovery and public publication are verified as separate delivery gates.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide
sections.text:
Fleetwright coordinates authorized browser operations through a durable control plane. Operators
review exact proposals; scoped MCP clients submit and investigate work; browser workers execute
approved actions; destination receipts establish outcomes. An interrupted action remains UNKNOWN
until evidence resolves it. A human review may be required indefinitely when a destination cannot
provide authoritative evidence.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide — Supported workflows
sections.text:
| Workflow | Contract | Success evidence |
| Freight booking | Published load reference and permitted destination account | Matching account booking receipt |
| Maintenance request | Stable reference, title and priority on the owned service portal | Matching account/reference/title/priority receipt |

Contracts define input constraints, account targets, preconditions, selectors, action paths,
destination statuses and reconciliation. A contract change invalidates the previous approval.
Adding a third workflow requires a reviewed contract and destination adapter, reconciliation proof,
authorization review and acceptance tests; arbitrary URLs/selectors are not accepted by MCP tools.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide — Operator and integration roles
sections.text:
Owners issue/revoke grants and approve exact actions. Operators inspect progress, investigate and
request safe cancellation. Viewers observe authorized information. Public access has restricted
controls and masked data; it cannot approve workflows or issue integration grants. MCP observation
and execution scopes remain separate and current authorization is checked on every invocation.

The hosted `/agent` page links to the separate local SQLite/Ollama application. Three maintained
owned templates draft maintenance, handover and inspection records, then require exact human
approval before a browser form save. Local state, private browser profile and receipts remain on
the owner's device. Optional CDP uses an isolated context and preserves existing tabs; it does
not inherit their logins. The hosted page does not control the local browser.

The console's catalogue crawler runs validated same-origin definitions with durable progress,
bounded HTTP egress, quality guards and private JSONL exports. Public visitors see aggregate state;
operators can start/cancel/export. See crawler and
local agent for supported behavior and limits.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide — Operator and integration roles
sections.text:
The dedicated MCP package supports model-supervised fleet workflows with the owner console.
Codex integration has end-to-end verification; Claude configuration and transport support are
documented, with account-level verification deferred. Implementation and release verification
are separate; consult the release record for what is currently deployed.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide — Delivery boundaries
sections.text:
Fleetwright includes its own freight board and service portal for controlled destination testing.
No relationship with a commercial freight marketplace is implied. Customer integrations require
written authorization and the onboarding checklist.

This repository is source-available under LICENSE. Public availability of source is
not a grant of unrestricted commercial use; review the license before distribution or resale.
Hosted service pricing, support agreements and contractual service levels are separate agreements.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide — Onboard an authorized workload
sections.text:
1. Establish the customer/tenant owner, destination permission, account scope and data purpose.
2. Select fleet workflow, catalogue crawler or local agent according to the actual action boundary.
3. Define allowed origins, fields/selectors, identity, rate budgets, retention and success/uncertainty receipts.
4. Provision private accounts and least-privilege grants; validate tenant isolation and owner approvals.
5. Exercise session expiry, rate limits, changed pages, interrupted acknowledgements and recovery.
6. Agree operating ownership, support, measured capacity and recovery objectives before production use.

The built-in destinations provide reproducible acceptance environments. New targets require their
own contract and review; an accessible page or a permissive robots file alone is not authorization.
See acceptable use, privacy and
security onboarding.

sections.heading: Fleetwright product guide — Choose the execution path
sections.text:
| Need | Execution path | Authority and state |
| Sustained coordinated freight work | Warm fleet actors and watchers | PostgreSQL claims, account pacing and cells |
| A reviewed business action | MCP proposal plus owner console | Versioned workflow approval and fenced worker |
| Approved structured data collection | Catalogue cycle | Durable frontier, extraction allowlist and private export |
| Local content drafting and form save | Standalone local agent | Installed model drafts; SQLite binds human approval and receipt |

Current verification includes 289 passing runtime regression cases with six expected skips, actual
driver/browser-loss recovery, exact release MCP/browser/crawler rehearsal and public workflows/UI/HTTP
with signed parity. Earlier installed-model flows and 50/70-context fixture hours retain their dated
boundaries. The current release record separates these results. These do not establish a
customer workload or availability SLA. Testing records their scope;
future scale and availability has explicit promotion gates.

sections.heading: Architecture overview
sections.text:
Fleetwright supervises complete browser workflows. PostgreSQL owns durable intent, authority and
outcomes; Redis accelerates dispatch and live updates; Playwright performs destination interaction.
The MCP server submits and investigates work without granting itself human approval.
