sections.heading: Architecture overview — Durable workflow protocol
sections.text:
Submission binds a stable action identity to tenant, account, exact inputs and the full contract
revision/hash. Reusing an identity with different content fails. Owner approval references that
fingerprint and expires by the database clock. A worker leases a job and account with a new fence,
then rechecks authorization immediately before committing `ACTING`. Only current fenced state
transitions can record results. The human approval is consumed for that execution.

Known destination rejection becomes `FAILED`. Response loss, process death or insufficient receipt
evidence becomes `UNKNOWN`. Expired pre-action leases can return to the ready queue; post-action
uncertainty cannot. Reconciliation reads destination receipts and checks the account and expected
action. Missing evidence does not establish failure. Persisted rotation prevents one old unknown
job from monopolizing reconciliation. Cancellation during uncertainty records intent and does not
claim to undo an external action. See the workflow runbook.

Fencing protects Fleetwright database authority; an arbitrary website does not consume that fence.
Correctness therefore also depends on the adapter's permitted action and receipt contract. Never
generalize controlled destination results into exactly-once delivery on all websites.

sections.heading: Architecture overview — Freight delivery and durable detections
sections.text:
Watchers capture bounded feed responses and persist raw detections before delivery. Filters/schedules select jobs;
claims and outbox rows commit together. The relay publishes to a cell stream. Warm actors lease,
act and record outcomes. The control reconciler examines uncertain bookings without blind retry.
Redis consumer groups reclaim interrupted deliveries; PostgreSQL unique constraints and fencing
remain authoritative. See claim lifecycle.
Raw detections remain in the PostgreSQL mailbox until their filter/claim decision commits. Tenant
moves reset unconsumed delivery under the directory lock, so unread old-cell streams and in-flight
messages are replayed using current authority. Legacy Redis-only upgrade data requires an explicit
drain; older backends cannot safely consume the new topic. See deployment.

sections.heading: Architecture overview — Isolation and evidence
sections.text:
Tenant content tables use PostgreSQL `ENABLE` and `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. Directory/system
lookups have narrow roles; shared infrastructure metadata is not represented as tenant content.
Target credentials and sessions use per-record envelope encryption and row-bound associated data.
Database mutations and their audit rows share a transaction. External Redis/HTTP operations persist
intent first and outcome afterward; unresolved intent remains inspectable after a crash.
Evidence exports are bounded/redacted canonical JSON with page hashes. Hashes detect changes;
they do not prove authorship. Browser artifacts may contain sensitive data and stay private.

sections.heading: Architecture overview — Scale boundaries
sections.text:
The freight engine has tenant-to-cell routing and Redis hash tags. The approved-workflow runner
uses bounded cell-scoped tenant pages and per-tenant turns, rechecking assignment before admission.
SSE-triggered refetch is coalesced; database pools and workflow scheduling must be
measured and redesigned at later milestones. A single-server deployment shares its host failure
domain. Multi-zone placement, gateway fleets, sharding and regional recovery remain
future architecture, with explicit decision records.

The stack is Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy/Alembic, PostgreSQL, Redis Streams, Playwright,
official FastMCP and Next.js/React. Lockfiles and deployment image digests define release versions.

sections.heading: Architecture overview — Three separate execution authorities
sections.text:
The fleet and general workflow runner share PostgreSQL authority, but use distinct process/account
lifecycles. Catalogue collection uses a fenced durable frontier and an allowlisted HTTP fetch
process; it does not give operators arbitrary browser scripting. The local agent uses SQLite on
the user's computer and an installed model for typed drafting; it does not depend on fleet services.

These boundaries prevent a model response, page instruction, Redis delivery or UI refresh from
becoming authority. Local edits survive polling but cannot authorize the old proposal; saving them
creates a new hash. Each uncertain action is reconciled against its destination contract.

sections.heading: Architecture overview — Operational failure domains
sections.text:
The host collector has administrative Docker authority solely for observe-only grant renewal;
the independent probe has neither execution nor approval access. Off-host recovery uses a separate
encryption key and proves data restoration without overwriting source databases. Those are distinct
from full-host/application recovery and measured availability.

Release identity includes committed source, immutable artifact inventory, final native app/web
image IDs and independently trusted signatures. Scan results are bound to those exact images.
Static rollback preserves compatible backends and mailbox state; backend recovery requires its
own tested compatibility procedure. See deployment,
monitoring and recovery.

sections.heading: Claim lifecycle
sections.text:
The claim state machine (`packages/fw_core/src/fw_core/claims.py`) is the part of Fleetwright that
enforces claim uniqueness, current fenced authority and explicit uncertain outcomes. Database
transitions combine with worker/adapter checks; external destinations do not validate database fences.
This does not guarantee exactly-once side effects on arbitrary websites.

sections.heading: Claim lifecycle — States
sections.text:
| State | Meaning | Who moves it |
| `QUEUED` | A detection matched a filter; one claim exists for the job | Dispatcher |
| `LEASED` | A claimer holds it with fencing token *n* until the lease expires | Claimer |
| `ACTING` | The claimer is sending the booking now | Claimer, only while its lease is current |
| `CONFIRMED` / `FAILED` | The target gave a definite answer | Claimer |
| `UNKNOWN` | The action may have happened but the answer is missing | Claimer (lost answer) or sweep (expired during `ACTING`) |
| `RECONCILED` | The reconciler checked the target and recorded what really happened | Reconciler |

sections.heading: Claim lifecycle — Rules
sections.text:
1. **One claim per job.** `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, target_job_key) DO NOTHING`. Exactly
   one detection wins, whatever the number of watchers.
2. **Fencing tokens.** Leasing takes `nextval('claim_fence')`. Every later step includes the token,
   and the `UPDATE` matches only if it is still current. A worker that paused (garbage collection,
   a frozen VM, a network stall) and woke up late is rejected.
3. **Database clock only.** Lease expiry compares against `clock_timestamp()` in Postgres. Worker
   clocks are measured (midpoint rule) for latency reporting but never trusted for correctness.
4. **Only claims that never reached `ACTING` are re-queued.** A claim whose lease expired while
   `LEASED` goes back to `QUEUED` (or `FAILED` when too old). A claim that expired while `ACTING`
   becomes `UNKNOWN`.
5. **`UNKNOWN` is never retried.** Retrying could book the job twice. The reconciler opens the
   account's sealed session, asks the target what the account has booked, and resolves the claim
   according to the destination receipt contract. An inconclusive absence remains uncertain for
   human investigation; a timeout alone is never evidence of rejection.
6. **A late actor still wins with the truth.** If the reconciler marked a claim `UNKNOWN` and the
   original actor then returns a definite answer with a still-current fence, that answer is
   recorded.
7. **One

sections.heading: Claim lifecycle — Rules
sections.text:
active lease per account.** A partial unique index prevents two concurrent actions on
   one target account.
8. **History and outbox in the same statement.** Each sweep rule is a single statement that moves
   the rows, writes `claim_events` and writes the outbox messages, so row locks are held for one
   round trip.

sections.heading: Claim lifecycle — Admission and detection durability
sections.text:
Account eligibility and database-clock pacing apply before admission and immediately before action.
Completion updates the cooldown; slow browser preparation cannot make the next action eligible early.
Watchers persist raw detections in a PostgreSQL mailbox before Redis delivery. Delivery alone does
not consume a detection: its filter/claim decision must commit. Tenant handover resets pending
routing under current directory authority and replays unread/in-flight old-cell work.

The unpublished-outbox metric does not include every published-but-unconsumed detection. Inspect
both durable backlog and stream pending/dead-letter state during a move or upgrade. See
ADR-012 and upgrade safety.

sections.heading: Claim lifecycle — Evidence
sections.text:
| Test | What it proves |
| 20-way lease race | Exactly one lease wins |
| Stale fence | An old token cannot move the claim |
| Crash while `LEASED` | The claim is re-queued and booked once |
| Crash while `ACTING` | The claim becomes `UNKNOWN` and is reconciled against the board |
| Hypothesis interleavings (40 generated schedules) | A terminal state never changes |
| 200 competitors × 10,000 jobs | 2026-10-13: 9,895 confirmed/reconciled claims and matching destination bookings; zero duplicate attempts |
| Engine chaos run (5xx errors, slow responses, lost acknowledgements, rival bots) | Every claim ends confirmed, failed or reconciled, and matches the board's ground truth |

sections.heading: ADR-001: Postgres is the claim authority; Redis is a fast path — Context
sections.text:
Two workers must never book the same job. Redis `SET NX PX` locks are fast, but a lock can expire
while its holder is paused (garbage collection, a frozen VM), and a failover can lose it. A second
worker then acts too.

sections.heading: ADR-001: Postgres is the claim authority; Redis is a fast path — Decision
sections.text:
Claims live in Postgres. A unique constraint on `(tenant_id, target_job_key)` picks the winner and a
fencing token from a sequence guards every later step. Redis is used only to drop obvious duplicates
early (`SET NX` per job) and to move messages quickly.

sections.heading: ADR-001: Postgres is the claim authority; Redis is a fast path — Consequences
sections.text:
- Correctness never depends on Redis. Losing a Redis cell loses speed, not safety.
- Each claim costs a few short Postgres transactions; this is the throughput limit to watch
  (see the capacity model).

sections.heading: ADR-002: A crash during the action is UNKNOWN, never a blind retry — Context
sections.text:
If a worker dies after sending a booking, nobody knows whether the booking happened. Retrying
could book twice; dropping could lose a job that was in fact booked.

sections.heading: ADR-002: A crash during the action is UNKNOWN, never a blind retry — Decision
sections.text:
A claim that expires in `ACTING` becomes `UNKNOWN`. The reconciler checks the target ("what has this
account booked?") with the account's own sealed session and records the truth as `RECONCILED`.

sections.heading: ADR-002: A crash during the action is UNKNOWN, never a blind retry — Consequences
sections.text:
- No duplicate bookings from retries.
- Needs a way to read back the account's bookings on every supported target. A target without one
  must be onboarded with an operator review step.

sections.heading: ADR-005: Cells: scale workers by adding independent units — Context
sections.text:
One Redis and one dispatcher cannot serve an unlimited number of workers, and one failure should
not stop every customer.

sections.heading: ADR-005: Cells: scale workers by adding independent units — Decision
sections.text:
A cell is one Redis plus its workers and control process. Each tenant is mapped to one cell in
`tenant_cells`; moving a tenant is a data change. Redis keys use `{tenant}` hash tags so a cell can
become a Redis Cluster later.

sections.heading: ADR-005: Cells: scale workers by adding independent units — Consequences
sections.text:
- Horizontal scale and fault isolation without code changes.
- A tenant larger than one cell needs the cell itself to scale (Redis Cluster, more workers).

sections.heading: ADR-009: What "1M users" and "99% uptime" mean here — Context
sections.text:
The owner asked for a design that can serve 1M+ simultaneous users with at least 99% uptime.
Fleetwright's users are operators; a million connected sessions only exists as a multi-tenant SaaS.
A million browser sessions would need about 100 TB of RAM, which is a different problem.

sections.heading: ADR-009: What "1M users" and "99% uptime" mean here — Decision
sections.text:
The control plane (API, console, live updates) is designed for 1M concurrent connected sessions
across many tenants. The worker plane is designed to grow by cells from tens to 10,000+ workers. The
availability target for the cloud reference is **99.9%** per month (stricter than the 99% asked for).
Nothing beyond what was measured is claimed as achieved.

sections.heading: ADR-009: What "1M users" and "99% uptime" mean here — Consequences
sections.text:
- The scaling docs separate *measured* from *target* numbers.
- The current single-server public workspace cannot meet either target and says so.

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users
sections.text:
The long-term product target is **at least 1,000,000 simultaneous connected console users**, across
many tenants, with separately budgeted automated browser capacity. This is a future architecture
and validation plan. The present deployment is a single server. Isolated verification sustained
50 and 70 Chromium contexts for separate uninterrupted hours, using a small owned fixture;
a separate 30-second control-plane test exercised 16 API and 32 SSE clients. These measurements
do not establish one-million-user capacity or representative destination throughput. See
the measured evidence and limitations.

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Workload contract
sections.text:
“Simultaneous” means authenticated/authorized sessions actively connected during a sustained test,
not registered accounts or a one-minute arrival count. The target test includes API reads/writes,
event fan-out, reconnects, tenant skew, slow clients, revoked users and an availability-zone failure.
One million browser contexts is a different workload; 100 MB per context would alone require
about 100 TB of memory. It is not the one-million-user control-plane target.

| Plane | Target workload | Main constraints |
| Static console | 1M+ simultaneous sessions | CDN cache misses, assets and regional delivery |
| API/authorization | Session, list, approval and investigation requests | Pool budget, query plans, per-tenant fairness and auth storage |
| Update gateway | 1M+ live connections | File descriptors, socket memory, event fan-out, bandwidth and reconnect storms |
| Execution | Independently scaled browser cells | Context memory/CPU, account exclusivity and destination permission/rate limits |
| Evidence | Bounded investigation and export | Retention, object storage, access control and retrieval cost |

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Delivery stages and exit gates
sections.text:
| Stage | Required implementation | Proof before promotion |
| Current single host | Hardened Compose, private data network, fenced jobs, immutable releases, backup tooling | Functional/adverse-condition suites and release rehearsal; no availability claim |
| Operational baseline | Verified archive/restore and monitoring tooling; independently operated availability checks and notifications | Full-host/key recovery, tested alert delivery and rolling 30-day SLI evidence; initial 99% operating objective |
| One region, multiple zones | Redundant API/gateways, database standby/PITR, isolated Redis cells, pooled connections, rolling releases | Zone-loss exercise under representative workload, no tenant crossover, 99.9% rolling objective |
| Many execution cells | Existing bounded cell-scoped tenant turns, account pacing/ownership and durable handover; expand deployment isolation | 50/70 fixture hours passed; next require representative approved workflows, tenant skew and cell-loss/rebalance under load |
| 1k to 100k connected users | Gateway sharding/fan-out, event coalescing, bounded refetch, reconnect jitter, read caches/replicas | Separate 1k, 10k and 100k sustained mixed-load tests, tenant skew and measured resource/cost curves |
| 1M+ connected users | Multi-zone gateway fleet, CDN, partitioned history, pooled database/read replicas, independent cells | At least 1M concurrent

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Delivery stages and exit gates
sections.text:
sessions sustained for an hour, representative actions/events, node/zone failures and measured SLOs |
| Regional recovery | Tested standby region, explicit writer authority and data residency | Recovery from regional loss with measured RPO/RTO; no automatic split-brain writes |

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Required engineering
sections.text:
Keep authoritative transitions in PostgreSQL. Pool application connections independently from
open HTTP connections; a million sessions must not imply a million database connections. Start
with measured query/index improvements and partition large histories before adopting sharding.
Sharding needs a tenant directory, migration protocol and explicit cross-shard limits.

Shard gateway subscriptions by tenant/channel, batch or coalesce invalidations and bound client
queues. Disconnect slow consumers with a recoverable cursor; provide resynchronization when the
cursor has expired. Spread reconnects with randomized backoff and throttle snapshot requests.
The current gateway and refetch behavior need load evidence before this design is promoted.

Current approved-workflow runners enumerate bounded tenant pages within their assigned cell and
take bounded turns. Account group eligibility, DB-clock pacing and durable handover are enforced.
Extend these controls with weighted tenant admission, deployment-level failure isolation and
representative fairness measurements. Scale by oldest eligible queue age and resource pressure,
within approved infrastructure and destination limits. Never create a retry storm around `UNKNOWN`
work. Redis delivery is transport; PostgreSQL retains action and raw-detection authority.

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Required engineering
sections.text:
Use zone-independent spare capacity so losing a zone does not depend on immediately provisioning
new capacity. Multi-region execution requires a single authoritative owner for an action and a
recovery protocol; geographic duplication alone does not establish safety.
This follows the spare-capacity principle in
AWS static stability.

Every milestone publishes concurrency, active tenants, request/event rates, payload sizes,
duration, hardware, resource limits, failure scenarios and percentile/error results. Cost estimates
require current provider quotes and owner approval before resources are provisioned.

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Architecture and decision records
sections.text:
The future service design defines the proposed routing, authorization,
data, fan-out and execution boundaries. Capacity arithmetic exposes the
assumptions behind resource and cost scenarios; the 500–1,000-user baseline
models the first realistic audience. Availability and recovery defines the
promotion objectives; adding a cell covers the current migration procedure.
The product roadmap owns delivery sequencing.

No cloud resources are created by these documents or the offline Terraform tests. Multi-zone
spare capacity, managed data services, regional traffic and evidence storage require a separately
reviewed operational budget; free-tier limits are not a capacity guarantee.

sections.heading: Scaling to 1M+ connected console users — Reproducible tier acceptance
sections.text:
The scale validation plan is the execution checklist for each future tier.
It defines preparation, steady traffic, tenant skew, reconnect/slow-reader pressure, zone loss,
restore and evidence publication. Tie the 99% operating objective and later 99.9% multi-zone objective
to a declared SLI window and owned error-budget policy.

Use measured bottlenecks to select the next infrastructure change. Record resource/cost scenarios
before approval, then verify the resulting topology against the same workload and failure gates.
Customer onboarding and data residency remain part of promotion, with responsibility assigned in
commercial readiness.

sections.heading: Security documentation
sections.text:
Fleetwright treats human authority, tenant isolation, destination permission and uncertain external
actions as separate security boundaries. The model proposes typed work; the operator approves
the exact account and inputs; database-backed authority governs execution and recovery.

| Document | Purpose |
| Control status | Implemented protections, release verification and operational responsibilities |
| Threat model | Assets, trust boundaries, attack scenarios and residual risks |
| ASVS assurance map | Selected OWASP ASVS 5 evidence, unassessed controls and explicit exceptions |
| Security reporting | Private vulnerability reporting and supported reporting scope |
| Privacy and legal register | Deployment-specific permission, data protection and incident obligations |
| Operations runbooks | Deployment, incident and recovery procedures |

Scan results apply to their exact source/image identities and scan time. Zero reported
HIGH/CRITICAL vulnerabilities does not establish absence of all vulnerabilities, an independent
penetration test or certification. The latest verified release evidence and remaining gates are
recorded in the assurance map; a newer release repeats relevant artifact gates.

sections.heading: Security documentation
sections.text:
Additions to destinations, model providers, permissions, storage or topology require a threat-model
and legal-scope review. Never submit private keys, account sessions, raw page traces or customer
records through a public issue.

sections.heading: Security documentation — Data, authority and operational handoff
sections.text:
Data lifecycle assigns handling requirements for identities, credentials,
workflow records, raw evidence, local profiles, exports and archives. Review it alongside the
threat model when adding a destination, provider, storage location or permission.

Security acceptance includes real role/CSRF/revocation behavior, tenant isolation, exact-action
approval, browser recovery, private evidence and verified backup/key recovery. Track unsupported
controls and retained advisories explicitly. Service ownership
and commercial readiness assign follow-up and incident duties.

sections.heading: Acceptable use and client onboarding gate
sections.text:
Fleetwright is a tool for automating web workflows **that the client is allowed to automate**.
These rules apply to private, customer and public workspace operation. Software licensing,
destination permission and a lawful processing purpose are separate onboarding requirements.

sections.heading: Acceptable use and client onboarding gate — Allowed
sections.text:
- Sites and systems the client owns or operates.
- Third-party sites whose terms permit automated access, or that have given the client written
  permission (for example, an API agreement or a partner programme).
- Testing and verification against the owned freight board in `apps/mockboard`.

sections.heading: Acceptable use and client onboarding gate — Not allowed
sections.text:
- Sites whose terms prohibit automation, without written approval from the site operator. Many
  freight load boards fall into this category.
- Bypassing logins, IP blocks, rate limits, captchas or other technical access controls.
- Using accounts the client does not own, shared or bought accounts, or credentials obtained
  without the account holder's consent.
- Collecting personal data without a lawful basis, or beyond what the task needs.
- Fake engagement, fake reviews, or AI-generated content presented as human without disclosure.
- Anything that degrades the target service (load beyond normal human-like use).

sections.heading: Acceptable use and client onboarding gate — Onboarding gate (required before any new destination)
sections.text:
No new destination is configured until every item is answered in writing and retained with its
scope/contract. The repository's license separately requires written permission
for production/commercial use or third-party-site access.

| # | Question | Evidence kept |
| 1 | Which site or platform, and which accounts? | Target list, account owners |
| 2 | Is automation allowed by its terms, or is there written permission? | Link to the terms clause, or the permission letter |
| 3 | Does it process personal data, and which basis/rights/risk-assessment duties apply? | Data inventory, assessed legal basis and DPIA where required; do not assume every task uses legitimate interests |
| 4 | Which hosting, model, proxy, OTP and other providers are used, with compatible permission/privacy terms? | Provider/subprocessor register; no CAPTCHA or access-control bypass |
| 5 | Data retention period and deletion process | Retention setting |
| 6 | Jurisdictions involved (client, target, data subjects, hosting) | Hosting region, transfer mechanism |
| 7 | Rate limits agreed with, or acceptable to, the target | Configured per-account limits |
| 8 | Who approves exact actions, handles uncertainty and revokes access? | Named authority, workflow contract, receipt/reconciliation and incident contacts |

**If question 2 cannot be answered with "yes", the project does not go ahead.**

sections.heading: Acceptable use and client onboarding gate — Operator responsibilities
sections.text:
Operators with console access must not change targets, accounts or rate limits outside what was
approved at onboarding. Every change is recorded in the tenant's audit log.

Stop affected admission when permission expires, an account is revoked, destination behavior
changes materially or execution becomes uncertain. Preserve evidence and reconcile accepted
actions before replacements. A working selector or login does not override permission boundaries.
Do not present generated reviews, identities or engagement as authentic human activity.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection
sections.text:
This describes current processing and the deployment obligations an operator must complete.
Owned destination records are maintained for workflow verification; operator identities, network
metadata and security logs can still be personal data. Do not treat an owned workspace as exempt
from privacy obligations.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Responsibility
sections.text:
The public site's operator determines its processing purposes. In a customer deployment,
controller/processor roles depend on actual decisions and contracts; they are not automatically
assigned by the software. Document roles, lawful basis, notices and a DPA where required before
processing customer data. Use the legal register for applicability and source links.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Data inventory
sections.text:
| Data | Purpose / storage | Current protection |
| Console email, role and password hash | Identity and authorization in PostgreSQL | Argon2id; role checks; encrypted TOTP secret |
| Target credentials/session state | Authorized destination login in account vault | Envelope encryption, row-bound associated data and tenant RLS |
| One-time codes | Login completion in memory/short-lived messaging | Limited lifetime, no intended log persistence |
| Freight/job/request inputs and receipts | Execution and reconciliation in PostgreSQL | Tenant isolation, exact-action fingerprint and bounded evidence |
| Approval/grant/session records | Human authority and client access | Expiry/revocation checks; stored token digests |
| Audit identity and network prefix | Investigation/accountability | Append-only application grants; IPv4 /24 or IPv6 /48 prefix in application audit |
| Browser screenshots/traces | Private failure investigation | Private storage and configured pruning; artifacts may contain page data |
| Database archives | Recovery | Restricted host permissions, verified manifests; archives remain sensitive |
| Help assistant questions and answers | Answering the asker in the console | Not stored by Fleetwright; kept only in the open page. Sent with retrieved documentation and read-only console data to the configured model provider (OpenRouter, routed only to providers that do not

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Data inventory
sections.text:
train on prompts); daily counters and a one-hour single-use feedback id hold no question text |

Edge, hosting and infrastructure access logs may have different network metadata than application
audit. Review their retention and vendor terms separately. Evidence redaction in JSON exports does
not establish that raw screenshots/traces or database archives are anonymous.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Retention and requests
sections.text:
Browser evidence has a configured retention period, seven days by default, and pruning in the
freight worker. Backup loop retention defaults to seven completed archives. Database job/audit
retention is not a complete automated deletion policy today. Before customer onboarding, assign
periods by category, legal holds, backup expiry, deletion ownership and verification. Restrict free
text and prohibit unnecessary sensitive personal data in workflow inputs.

Handle access, correction, deletion and objection requests through the deployment operator:
verify identity/authority, identify the tenant and records, assess legal retention duties, export
or correct/delete through an approved procedure, and record completion. Append-only audit records
need a legally reviewed minimization/pseudonymization policy; do not promise automatic deletion
that is not implemented. Apply the applicable jurisdiction's deadline and extensions.

Maintain an operator request register with receipt date, verified requester/authority, applicable
jurisdiction, affected categories, legal holds, deadline, decision and completion evidence.
Processing-record duties are separate from permission to retain all raw personal data. Apply the
current Bangladesh Act and jurisdiction-specific requirements where relevant;
older ordinance summaries are not the current legal baseline.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Retention and requests
sections.text:
Deletion must account for rows, caches, browser profiles, screenshots/traces, exports and archive
expiry. Where a protected archive is retained for recovery, restrict access, record expiry and
reapply approved minimization/deletion decisions after restoration. Preserve necessary legal or
incident evidence under an assessed hold; indefinite retention is not a security control.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Cookies, providers and transfers
sections.text:
The application uses necessary session/CSRF mechanisms and local browser preferences; no application
advertising or analytics integration is configured. Hosting/CDN providers may apply their own
security mechanisms. Document subprocessors and hosting regions in a deployment-specific notice.
International transfer safeguards require an assessed legal mechanism and contract; choosing a
region or provider does not by itself complete that assessment.

MCP exports exclude credentials, cookies, arbitrary payloads and raw page HTML. Client prompts
and model-provider retention are outside that export boundary: send only necessary redacted
material and review the selected provider's terms. There is no automatic paid model API fallback.

The standalone agent keeps private local state/history and uses a dedicated profile or isolated
CDP context. Its configured
local Ollama flow avoids a hosted model API for that path, but destination submissions still leave
the device. CDP connection, exports, remote destinations and any newly selected provider each need
assessment; local inference is not a promise that all processing remains local.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Cookies, providers and transfers
sections.text:
Before deployment, publish the actual operator identity/contact, purposes and legal bases,
retention schedule, rights channels, recipients/subprocessors and transfer safeguards. This
engineering inventory is not a completed deployment-specific privacy notice or DPA.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Help assistant provider
sections.text:
The console help assistant sends the visitor's question, recent turns of the same conversation,
matching documentation passages and read-only data the visitor's role can already see to the
configured model API (currently OpenRouter). The request asks the router to use only providers
that do not collect prompts for training. Provider-side retention, subprocessors and transfer terms
are the provider's; review them before a customer deployment and do not enable the assistant for
regulated data without a processing agreement. Operators can switch it off (`FW_ASSISTANT__ENABLED`),
which leaves documentation search working.

sections.heading: Privacy and data protection — Security incidents
sections.text:
Contain unauthorized access, preserve private evidence, identify affected data and notify the
responsible controller/operator promptly. GDPR controller notification to a supervisory authority
is generally within 72 hours where required; processor notification is without undue delay.
Other jurisdictions can differ. Follow incident response.

sections.heading: Catalogue crawling
sections.text:
An operator or owner can start an approved catalogue cycle from **Console → Crawl jobs**. The
console shows durable progress, extraction errors, change counts and quality alerts. Exports contain
only the configured allowed fields. Public visitors can inspect aggregate progress; submission,
cancellation and export require an authenticated operator role and mutations require CSRF.

Start the worker with `uv run python -m fw_coordinator.crawls`. Apply database migrations first.
The release template supervises the crawler independently from freight and approved browser jobs.
The API and crawler share the private export volume. The local environment template documents
all `FW_CRAWL__*` settings; deployment settings control the volume path and resource limits.

Definitions live in `config/crawls.yaml`: approved origin name, seed paths, JSON Pointer or CSS row
selector, optional next-page selector, field allowlist/types/lengths, identity field and robots
policy. Arbitrary operators cannot submit selectors or destinations through the API. Additional
public origin URLs belong to typed `FW_CRAWL__ORIGINS`; they receive no private-address exception.
Review destination authorization and network egress before enabling one.

sections.heading: Catalogue crawling
sections.text:
Robots are respected by default. Robots errors fail closed; redirects are refused. Requests have
response-size and time bounds. Shared per-origin admission, bounded retries and a durable failed
frontier prevent an unbounded retry loop. Cancellation finishes at the next bounded page boundary.
An expired lease is recovered with a new fence, retaining pages already committed.

A layout change can produce an extraction failure or result-drop alert. Inspect the maintained
contract and destination before running another cycle. An incomplete cycle does not report old
unseen items as removed. JSONL exports for failed cycles contain only records actually extracted
in that cycle. Missing identity/type/length data causes page failure rather than silent truncation.

The configured retention period deletes old export files, corresponding frontier data and old
current-item rows. Run the worker regularly for retention enforcement. Backups have their own
retention policy; deleting an export does not erase data from previously retained database archives.

The owned catalogue provides a stable, paginated target. Its alternate layout exercises the quality
alarm. It is separate from the live freight feed. External webhooks, paid proxy/captcha services and
Parquet/S3 delivery are not enabled in this release; use the private JSONL export interface.

sections.heading: Catalogue crawling — Inspect, export and investigate
sections.text:
The API exposes maintained definitions, paginated jobs, operator submission/cancellation and
tenant-bound exports; see integration routes and generated OpenAPI. The native
console path is select catalogue → Start crawl → inspect progress → Download JSONL. Exports are
no-store responses and expire under configured retention.

Before accepting a cycle, check its terminal state, extracted item count, errors, added/changed/
removed counts and alerts. A failed export is partial evidence, not a complete catalogue snapshot.
Investigate zero-result/drop alerts before consuming downstream removals. Keep field types and
identity constraints synchronized with the destination.

The real owned catalogue flow reaches COMPLETE and exports four exact records across two pages.
Tests also exercise TLS hostname verification, numeric DNS pinning, malformed/truncated JSON,
physical termination of slow fetches, stale fences, cancellation and cross-tenant/export denial.
The subprocess boundary confirms over-budget network work exits before retrying; cancelling only
an await is insufficient. See test evidence.

sections.heading: Catalogue crawling — Network and privacy policy
sections.text:
Only explicitly configured owned origins may receive private-address access. Additional origins
retain public-address restrictions. DNS validation/pinning, TLS hostname checks, refusal of redirects
and independent byte/time/page budgets constrain the supported HTTP path; do not claim a general
purpose network sandbox. Review lawful collection, personal-data minimization and retention before
adding a destination. See privacy and acceptable use.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows
sections.text:
Fleetwright coordinates complete authorized workflows around its existing freight engine.
The second owned workflow creates a maintenance request on the owned freight board's `/portal` page.
Both use the same destination account vault but have different forms, payloads and receipt checks.
Neither requires a paid model API or a third-party account.

Authentication contracts are separate from freight contracts: a service-only target can supply
login and identity checks without inventing freight endpoints. Legacy freight workers filter
their account acquisition to freight-capable targets. These adapters remain restricted to the
configured owned origin; this is not arbitrary-site browser execution.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Start and authorize
sections.text:
1. Install the locked workspace (`uv sync --frozen`) and Playwright Chromium. Start the local
   data stack, owned freight board and coordinator using the existing development instructions.
2. Run `python -m fw_coordinator.migrate`. Apply every current migration; workflow, crawler, pacing and durable-detection changes have
   separate compatibility requirements described in deployment.
3. Sign in as a real owner with password and TOTP. The shared workspace account cannot approve
   or issue access grants. `POST /v1/workflow-grants` accepts `{"scopes":["observe","execute"]}`
   with the authenticated cookie and session CSRF header. Use observation alone for investigation.
4. Save the returned tenant ID and short-lived token as `FW_MCP__TENANT_ID` and
   `FW_MCP__ACCESS_TOKEN` in the gitignored local environment, and record the actual recovery
   values in the already-ignored credentials file. Never put tokens into CLI arguments,
   client JSON/TOML, prompts, evidence, or source control. A grant is limited by
   `FW_WORKFLOWS__GRANT_TTL_S`; revocation is immediate on the next tool call.
5. Configure a stdio client, then run `python -m fw_worker.workflows` separately. The MCP server
   submits durable proposals; the supervised worker performs approved browser actions.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Start and authorize
sections.text:
The owner API also supports `DELETE /v1/workflow-grants/{grant_id}` and
`DELETE /v1/workflows/jobs/{job_id}/approval`. All mutations require CSRF. The API contract is
generated in `contracts/openapi.yaml`.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Claude and Codex
sections.text:
Run each server in the workspace directory so typed settings load its private `.env`. Use the
workspace's Python executable, not an unrelated global interpreter. On Windows select the
virtual environment under `Scripts`; on Linux select the executable under `bin`.

Codex host/project configuration:

Claude project configuration:

`python` above must resolve to the activated workspace environment. Alternatively set `command`
to that environment's executable and configure the server working directory in the client.
Client configuration contains no secret values. Use the current client's installed model and
subscription settings; do not silently fall back to paid APIs.

Ask the client to list contracts, then submit a stable action identity, workflow ID, permitted
account ID and exactly the required inputs. `workflow_contracts` returns field constraints.
Reuse the same identity only for the same action. Changing input under an existing identity is
rejected. Missing or disabled accounts are denied.

Official setup references: Codex MCP,
Claude MCP, MCP tools specification.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Human review and outcome
sections.text:
Open **Console → Browser workflows**, refresh, and review a proposal. The screen shows the
destination account, exact inputs and action fingerprint. An owner must check the review box
before approving. An operator may inspect and request cancellation but cannot approve.
The fingerprint includes tenant, account, full input and complete contract revision/hash.
Set-valued contract fields are sorted before hashing, so independent coordinator and worker
processes compute the same identity. An eight-seed subprocess regression verifies this boundary.
Workers recheck approval, grant, current roles, account state and DB-clock lease immediately
before committing ACTING. Changed, expired, revoked or already-consumed approvals cannot act.

Cancellation before ACTING safely terminates the job. Cancellation during ACTING or UNKNOWN
records intent without claiming the destination action was undone. A worker death after ACTING
becomes UNKNOWN on lease expiry. UNKNOWN is never selected for another click. Fair, persisted
reconciliation rotates through old and new unknown jobs without changing their outcome age.
Missing receipts are inconclusive on these two destinations; they do not authorize a retry.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Human review and outcome
sections.text:
Expired approval on a queued job prevents execution. Cancel it and create a separately reviewed
proposal if the pre-action state is known; never use this procedure for UNKNOWN work.
An unavailable/expired destination session can leave a job UNKNOWN for operator investigation.
No exactly-once promise is made for arbitrary websites or destinations without verifiable receipts.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Evidence and monitoring
sections.text:
Inspect a job and download its evidence in the console, or call `export_evidence`. Follow
`next_cursor` to retrieve later pages. Job listing is also paginated. Exports contain bounded
state transitions, fences, safe status/reason codes and receipt hashes, excluding credentials,
raw page HTML, cookies and arbitrary payloads. Each page has a SHA-256 hash over canonical JSON:
this detects content changes; it is not a signature or proof of who authored an export.

Authenticated operators can read `/v1/workflows/health`. Prometheus-compatible metrics at
`/v1/workflows/metrics` require an observation bearer grant and `X-Fleetwright-Tenant` header.
They report state counts, freight unknowns, pending outbox rows and alert counts. Old UNKNOWN
outcomes and stalled queued work have actionable alerts. Thresholds and operational bounds live
in typed workflow settings; operator messages and workflow definitions live in validated YAML.
Do not expose the metrics endpoint anonymously or include grant tokens in scrape logs.

Console database mutations and audit records share a transaction. External Redis/HTTP actions
record intent before action and outcome afterward, leaving visible unresolved intent on a crash.
Live streams recheck session authorization, including while idle, at the configured
`FW_GATEWAY__REVOCATION_CHECK_S` interval.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Backup and restore
sections.text:
Configure `FW_BACKUP__*` through the typed settings and private environment. The host-side
backup command uses the existing Docker CLI and database container, with credentials retained
inside the database environment. `python -m fw_coordinator.backup create` writes custom-format
PostgreSQL archives, verifies their contents and records hashes. A failed backup does not remove
the last good backup. `loop` repeats at the configured interval and keeps the configured number
of completed backups; supervise it using the host's service manager and a protected backup location.

`python -m fw_coordinator.backup drill <backup-folder>` verifies hashes before restoring into
new uniquely named databases ending in `_restore_test`. It refuses existing targets and never
drops development or production databases. Database archives do not contain cluster roles:
bootstrap the repository's role setup first when restoring onto a new cluster, using private
current passwords. Protect archives as secrets and copy them to an independently protected
destination using the operator's approved backup policy.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Backup and restore
sections.text:
The automated drill restores into a fresh network-isolated cluster and checks the approved job,
approval, events and audit. That is stronger evidence than counting tables in the source cluster.
The readiness probe waits for loopback TCP: the official image temporarily accepts Unix-socket
connections during initialization before shutting down that server. A delayed-initialization
regression verifies the final server is ready before one-time role bootstrap and restoration.
The 13 October release also verifies the protected production
scheduler, current-release process directory and archive/source integrity. These checks do not
establish off-site backup retention or full-host recovery.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Verification
sections.text:
The historical reliable-browser extension met 14/14 acceptance criteria for the owner-adjusted scope:
Claude's actual client run is explicitly deferred; Codex's actual run passed for both workflows.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Verification
sections.text:
| Gate | Verified result |
| Backend behavior | Final regression run:147passed; unchanged contention benchmark separately passed in205.19s (previous full147-case run:546.13s), including the unchanged 200-worker/10,000-job contention benchmark and corrected fresh-cluster restore regression |
| Python lint / formatting / types | Ruff clean, 160 files formatted; mypy clean on 66 source files |
| Dashboard | ESLint, TypeScript and production build passed |
| Packaging / configuration | All eight Python wheel/sdist builds and Compose configuration passed; settings/config regressions passed |
| Security | Bandit medium+ clean; Gitleaks history and public working snapshot clean; Semgrep117rules/276targets, zero findings/errors |
| Dependency audit | Patched MCP SDK 1.28.1: Python audit clean; npm production audit clean. Full npm audit retains the development-only advisory described below |
| Real workflows | Freight and maintenance portal, interrupted acknowledgement, OS-killed worker after acceptance, receipt reconciliation, owner approval and evidence download passed |
| Operations | Idle-stream revocation, authenticated metrics, scheduled backup, corrupt-archive refusal and isolated fresh-cluster restoration passed |
| Client / independent review | Actual Codex submission/result/export passed; fresh-context review approved after all reported defects were fixed |

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Verification
sections.text:
An earlier full run timed out in the legacy load benchmark before its final assertions. The
unchanged isolated rerun passed; the original 900-second deadline and coverage were preserved.
The timeout's root cause was not conclusively established. Deployment is verified separately in
the release evidence; representative authenticated fleet capacity remains unproven.

Full npm audit is **not clean**: the development-only Next ESLint dependency chain includes
`braces` 3.0.3, affected by GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm.
The advisory and npm registry currently provide no patched release. Independent review found
the identified call handles repository `settings.next.rootDir` patterns, which this project does
not configure, and found no application runtime import. The finding is retained, with no audit
suppression or framework downgrade. Reassess when a fix appears or lint tooling accepts untrusted
patterns. This is an explicit limitation of local acceptance.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Verification
sections.text:
Run `python tools/dev/run_tests.py -q` against isolated test databases. Build the dashboard before
the console browser gate. The harness serializes runs so one cannot reset another's destination.
The tests cover worker contention, stale fences, killed processes after acceptance, response loss,
changed/expired/replayed approval, tenant isolation, immediate revocation, bounded redaction,
atomic audit, fair recovery and fresh-cluster restoration. The separate private Codex verification
script is an explicit manual subscription check, not a CI test or paid API fallback.

Claude's live verification is deferred at the owner's request because its subscription is off.
Keep client setup and transport verification separate from claims about an actual model-driven run.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Configuration and secret audit
sections.text:
The final working-source and Git-history scans found no real secrets. Private credentials,
environment files, memory and browser/backup artifacts are ignored and absent from tracked
history. Typed settings and both environment templates cover the added execution, approval,
grant, pagination, reconciliation, stream-revocation and backup bounds. Automated configuration
regressions reject provider URLs, model IDs and obvious secret patterns in backend source.

Workflow descriptions, selectors, paths, input constraints, destination statuses, server
instructions and operator messages live in validated YAML. Deployment URLs, timeouts, storage,
credentials and operational limits live at the settings boundary. Stable API routes, state/scope
names, SQL identifiers, cryptographic primitives and fixed input/evidence safety caps remain
protocol definitions; changing a destination workflow requires configuration rather than editing
the execution state machine.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Account pools in the release
sections.text:
The seed provisions a dedicated `workflow` account group alongside the four freight accounts.
`FW_WORKER__RESERVED_ACCOUNT_GROUPS` excludes that group from long-lived freight slot acquisition.
Choose the approved-workflow account when submitting jobs; accounts occupied by freight slots remain
unavailable until released. This prevents the two supervised workers from monopolizing each other's
capacity. Keep reserved groups aligned with the seed configuration.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Current browser recovery and readiness
sections.text:
The 14 October correction, retained and reverified in the 15 October publication release,
supervises the Chromium connection with a bounded read-only protocol
roundtrip and disconnect callback. Driver/browser loss triggers resource drain and process exit
for the existing supervisor. Only connected, ready slots report running; starting slots remain stale.
The typed heartbeat interval and action timeout own the probe cadence/deadline. The CDP method
name is fixed protocol syntax. Actual child termination recovered four ready slots in one restart;
strict normal SIGTERM still exits 0 with all holds released. Public bookings and both approved
workflows passed. See the current release record.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Historical 13 October completion verification and lifecycle
sections.text:
The final completion regression passed 274 tests with six expected skips in 762.41 seconds;
all 435 source/tool hashes remained unchanged. Exact rc4 release rehearsal
includes both real MCP workflows, owner review/evidence, crawler and responsive console flows.
Separate installed-model local-agent proof and 50/70-context owned-fixture hours broaden the evidence;
they do not establish arbitrary destination correctness or authenticated fleet capacity.

The final rc4 rehearsal passed actual freight drain with four stopped slots and zero held accounts,
a controlled 12-second workflow drain, and crawler SIGTERM exit 0/non-OOM with its exact container
restored. All three configured container grace periods are 60 seconds. A separate-process crawler
resumed only after natural lease expiry; static-only rollback preserved pending durable detections
and backend identities. These are exact rehearsal proofs; deployed rc4 separately passed public
MCP/UI/HTTP and running-image/artifact parity checks.

Before dependency/service replacement, gracefully stop the freight worker, workflow worker and
crawler when present. Verify all stop graces exceed application drain bounds and record successful
non-OOM exits and released holds. Keep old control available through legacy stream drain, then
stop control and take a fresh archive before migration. See deployment and
operational runbooks.

sections.heading: Reliable browser workflows — Historical 13 October completion verification and lifecycle
sections.text:
Operational collection and independent encrypted recovery now have dedicated implementations and
proof boundaries; use monitoring and recovery instead of treating a
local scheduled archive as complete host-loss protection. Final installation and live evidence
belong in the release record.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent
sections.text:
The standalone application runs on the owner's machine with SQLite, Playwright Chromium and an
already-installed local Ollama model. It uses neither the fleet's PostgreSQL/Redis services nor a
Docker runtime. No cloud model, API key or paid service is required or enabled.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Start and use
sections.text:
1. Install the workspace with `uv sync`, then install Chromium with `python -m playwright install chromium`.
2. Start Ollama with an already-installed model. Set `FW_AGENT__MODEL_ID` to its exact installed name.
   The application refuses cloud-suffixed models, models absent from local inventory, remote-backed
   model metadata, redirects and non-numeric/non-loopback model endpoints.
3. Copy the agent group from `.env.example` into the local ignored `.env`. The typed boundary owns
   the model URL/name, database/profile/evidence paths, loopback host/port, destination origins,
   headless setting, deadlines, body/content/model/tab/action/approval budgets and optional CDP URL.
   `FW_AGENT__HISTORY_LIMIT` controls how many recent tasks the UI/API lists, newest first; older
   records remain in SQLite and can still be retrieved by their identifiers.
4. Run `python -m fw_agent` from the repository root. Open the exact HTTP origin defined by the
   configured numeric loopback host and port. The API deliberately rejects alternate Host headers,
   remote clients, cross-site requests and mutation requests without same-origin CSRF authorization.
5. Select a template and explicit destination, describe the draft, and choose **Read pages and draft
   locally**. Wait for `AWAITING_APPROVAL`; inspect the source, final draft, full proposal and hash.
6. Edit the draft if necessary. Saving

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Start and use
sections.text:
edits cancels the old proposal and creates a new proposal/hash.
   **Approve this exact save** consumes one unexpired approval. Download the receipt after confirmation.
7. Use **Cancel task** or **Stop all agent tasks** to halt work. The global stop requires application
   restart before new tasks can start. An action interrupted after approval becomes `UNKNOWN`.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Three maintained workflows
sections.text:
| Template | Source tab | Destination tab | Effect |
| Maintenance request | Owned equipment status | Maintenance draft form | Saves an owned local record |
| Dispatch handover note | Owned dispatch status | Handover draft form | Saves an owned local record |
| Inspection summary | Owned inspection observations | Inspection draft form | Saves an owned local record |

The lab is enabled explicitly by configuration. These are functional owned workflows;
they do not send emails, post publicly, buy anything or integrate with a third-party production app.
Other explicitly authorized origins can be configured only when they implement the same strict form
and receipt contract. This is not an arbitrary-site autonomous agent. CAPTCHA/login bypass is absent.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Approval and uncertainty
sections.text:
SQLite WAL with full synchronous durability is the action authority. SHA-256 binds the complete
template snapshot, origin, request, captured source and final title/body. Approval is atomically
consumed before browser execution. Expired, replayed and changed approvals are refused. Changing a
template after a proposal was created also requires a fresh proposal. Approval cannot be emitted by
the model: its schema contains only `title` and `body`, with extra fields forbidden.

`PREPARING → AWAITING_APPROVAL → ACTING → CONFIRMED` is the normal flow. Interrupted actions become
`UNKNOWN`, including `ACTING` rows found at application restart. The agent never blindly resubmits
an UNKNOWN action. **Check destination receipt** performs a read only. A receipt must match the task
identifier, hash, title and body before confirmation. Missing or mismatched receipts retain UNKNOWN
for human investigation. The owned lab records one idempotent receipt for each exact task.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Browser and local API boundary
sections.text:
Dedicated persistent profiles are the default. Only that application's profile pages are controlled.
Optional loopback CDP attaches to Chromium and creates a new isolated context; it deliberately does
not inherit the owner's existing tabs or login. Closing the agent closes its own context and stops
the Playwright connection. It does not call `browser.close()` on the owner's attached browser.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Browser and local API boundary
sections.text:
The agent uses two tabs and nine explicit navigation/fill/click interactions for a complete template.
The title/body wire schema, identifier formats, hash serialization and named adapter interaction
cost are versioned protocol constraints; deployment limits come from the central settings boundary.
Waits, reads and evidence capture have bounded timeouts. Context routing blocks other origins,
and a configured request ceiling bounds each prepare, execute or reconciliation phase. It blocks
preapproval mutations, popup navigation and all mutation payloads except the single exact approved
POST to the maintained template's accept path. Service workers are blocked.
WebSockets are denied for the entire dedicated/isolated-CDP context lifetime, before task pages
are opened; rejection does not connect to the remote WebSocket server. HTTP request routing alone
does not cover that transport. The model cannot choose selectors, URLs or operations.
Destination page text remains untrusted reference material; this
constrains authority even if the model repeats poisoned prose. Human content review remains necessary.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Browser and local API boundary
sections.text:
The UI uses same-site HTTP-only session cookies, same-origin CSRF tokens, strict Host/client/Origin
checks, bounded bodies, no CORS wildcard, a self-only content security policy and no-store responses.
Loopback HTTP is intentional; remote exposure/reverse proxying is unsupported. Local hostile software
with access to the same user account is outside this boundary. Keep the SQLite database, profile,
screenshots and receipt exports private: they can contain the source and human draft.
On POSIX, the application restricts its owned state/profile/evidence directories to0700 and state
files to0600, including SQLite WAL/SHM. It preserves existing content while tightening permissions
and refuses symlink or foreign-owned state paths. Use dedicated directories for these paths.
Windows inherits the chosen directory's ACLs; POSIX mode checks do not establish Windows ACL privacy.

These application-level HTTP/WebSocket controls are not an operating-system network sandbox.
Other browser channels such as WebRTC, WebTransport and DNS are not claimed to be constrained by
Playwright HTTP routing. Use only owned or expressly authorized contract pages; do not use this
application to execute arbitrary hostile sites. Isolating hostile executable pages requires an
independent OS/container egress policy, which this lightweight standalone runtime does not install.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Verification and recovery
sections.text:
`pytest -q packages/fw_agent/tests -m 'not slow'` runs authority, API and real Chromium tests without
a local model. `pytest -q packages/fw_agent/tests --agent-model-proof` additionally exercises all three
templates with the installed local model and prints its private local evidence directory.
CI does not claim to have an installed model: that one proof skips unless explicitly requested.

After power loss, restart the application against the same SQLite database and profile. Review
UNKNOWN tasks and reconcile
receipts; never delete task rows to force a retry. JSON evidence records the exact approval hash and
matching receipt; screenshots show the destination acknowledgement.

sections.heading: Standalone local browser agent — Model and review maintenance
sections.text:
The installed model is selected by typed settings, not by task text. The adapter checks local
inventory and remote-backed metadata, requests a strict title/body JSON schema, bounds model
response size/tokens/time, and supplies no action tools. See the
official structured chat format.

Treat page content and model prose as untrusted. Review both title and body, including any
unsupported inference. Unsaved fields survive blur, manual refresh and polling; approval refuses
them until Save edits produces a new proposal. Confirm that the final receipt matches the reviewed
content rather than checking only the CONFIRMED label.

For upgrades, stop active tasks, preserve the SQLite/profile/evidence directories, back up private
state and inspect UNKNOWN tasks after restart. Re-run approval, cancellation, injection and
two-origin HTTP/WebSocket tests when changing templates or browser policy. Actual installed-model
proof is separate from default CI; POSIX permission checks do not establish Windows ACL privacy.
